On the ninth day after the river came through, we opened a lost-property office in the high school gym. We had six folding tables, a pad of claim forms, and a rule against plugging anything in. By noon somebody had plugged in a lamp. It worked. For the rest of the week people brought things over to see them in its light, though the gym was perfectly bright.

The first thing I tagged was a wooden spoon. I wrote FOUND AT CORNER OF THIRD AND ELM, which made it sound as if the spoon had been waiting for a bus. Later, when we ran out of tags, we wrote directly on things. A white refrigerator door said BEHIND THE LIBRARY in blue marker.

The door had no refrigerator attached. It lay flat across two milk crates, and people rested their coffee on it while filling out forms. On Friday a woman in a green raincoat came in, saw it, and said, “Oh, good.”

She turned it over. Three mugs hit the floor. One broke.

“Sorry,” she said, without looking up.

On the other side were pencil lines, dates, and names. Some of the lines had been drawn over so many times that the pencil had scored the enamel. The lowest one said JUNE, SHOES ON.

“That’s mine,” she said.

The claim form asked for an identifying feature not visible to staff. I asked her if there was anything written under the rubber seal.

“How would I know?”

“Sometimes people put things there.”

“Do they?”

I had no idea. I lifted the seal with my thumbnail. A little brown water came out.

June, it turned out, was her sister. The woman was Ruth, which was also the name beside most of the lines. There were a few for a boy called Ian, and one, nearly six feet up, for a visiting cousin whose arrival had apparently been an event.

“My mother started it on the kitchen wall,” Ruth said. “Then she painted the kitchen.”

Her mother was in a motel off the interstate, in a room with a microwave on top of a microwave. The first one didn’t work. Ruth had asked the manager why he didn’t take it away, and he said the second one would be too low.

I got as far as writing Ruth’s name on the form before a man at the end of the table said, “That came off my fridge.”

We looked at him. He had been in every day that week. He’d found one of his lawn chairs on Tuesday and had kept coming back because, as he explained, he used to have two.

“Mine had that dent,” he said, pointing to the bottom corner of the door.

Ruth pointed to her name.

“I see that,” he said. “I’m not saying it makes sense.”

He took out his phone. He had a picture of his dog asleep in front of a refrigerator with a dent in the bottom corner. It was a very good picture of the dog. You couldn’t see much of the refrigerator.

“Did you buy it used?” Ruth asked.

The man thought about it. “I got it from a lady on Spruce.”

“That’s my mother.”

In the gym behind us, somebody dropped a drawer full of cutlery. We waited for the noise to die down.

“She told me she put it out for the scrap man,” Ruth said.

“No. I gave her sixty dollars.”

Ruth ran her finger along one of the pencil lines. I thought she might ask him why he’d left them there. Instead she asked if the fridge had worked.

“For four years,” he said. “Freezer was terrible.”

“Yes,” she said. “It was.”

I put the claim form between them. The man looked down at the box marked REPLACEMENT VALUE and laughed. Then he asked Ruth whether she’d seen a green lawn chair anywhere near the library. She hadn’t, but she asked what kind of green, and he said the kind that starts out green and gets whiter every summer. She said she’d keep an eye out.

The door was too wide for the trunk of her car. We lowered the back seats and slid it in from the passenger side. Halfway through, Ruth said, “Hang on,” and I thought we’d caught a hinge on something. But she was looking at a line near the top.

“October,” she said. “I must have been home from college.”

It was higher than the one before it by less than the width of the pencil mark.

“She said I hadn’t grown,” Ruth said. “I made her do it again.”

There was, if you leaned in, a second line.

When we got back inside, the man was on his knees with a dustpan, sweeping up the mug. He’d put the two that hadn’t broken on my chair. One was his.

“Sorry about the table,” Ruth said.

“It wasn’t a very good table,” I told her. This was untrue. It had been exactly the height you wanted a table to be.

On Monday she came back with the door. She and her mother had taken pictures of all the marks. Her mother wanted to know whether she’d be charged for leaving it with us.

“People have been setting their coffee on the floor,” I said.

We put the door back on its crates, writing side down. Ruth pressed on each corner to make sure it wouldn’t tip. Then she took a pencil from the box of claim forms and crouched beside it. I could hear the pencil moving but couldn’t see what she wrote.

After she left, I got down on my knees and looked. On the underside of the door, beside JUNE, SHOES ON, Ruth had written the name of the gym and the date. The pencil had barely taken. I had to turn my head sideways to read it.
